land.text: the northern and central lowlands kept in Cliopatria's 850 shape

predecessors.note: The southern and highland kingdoms in the 840 shape pass to nobody.

land.text: the northern Yucatan Peninsula conquered in 1527-1546
the Itza kingdom of the Peten, independent to 1697

successors.note: Cliopatria's Itza row begins in 1547; the Itza had held Nojpeten since the mid-15th century.

capitals.name: Chichen Itza
capitals.note: 'Between 900 and 1050 AD Chichen Itza expanded to become a powerful regional capital controlling north and central Yucatan'; it 'declined as a regional center by 1100'; the last known date at the site is 998. Label anchor from 850 (Uxmal, Calakmul and Tikal were the other Terminal Classic seats).

capitals.name: Mayapan
capitals.note: Capital 'from the 1220s until the 1440s'; written records give the abandonment as 1441, archaeology about 1461. After the fall no page names a common seat.

keyframe_review.note: 177,291 km2 for 850-869: the northern lowlands plus the central Peten (Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque) once the southern kingdoms (about 749 cells: Copan, Caracol, Quirigua, the Usumacinta and Pasion kingdoms, the highlands) are gone. The page has 'population centers continued in many coastal regions and in the northern Yucatan Peninsula, including Chichen Itza, Uxmal, and Coba' and Tikal's last stela is 869 (Tikal page), so keeping Tikal and Calakmul is right. No infobox area exists to compare.

Same cells as 850 (177,291 km2). Calakmul's Stela 61 is dated 899 or 909 and Tikal 'was all but deserted' after 950 (Tikal and Calakmul pages), so the shape can run to 959; the page itself says only that the central capitals were 'generally abandoned within a period of 50 to 100 years' of the collapse.

135,191 km2: the shape loses about 162 cells of the central lowlands (Tikal, El Mirador, Uaxactun, Palenque), leaving the northern Yucatan, Calakmul and northern Belize. Matches 'Palenque, Copan, Tikal, and Calakmul went into decline during the 8th and 9th centuries and were abandoned shortly thereafter', though the page dates none of it; the Chichen Itza page has Chichen Itza 'a powerful regional capital controlling north and central Yucatan' in 900-1050 inside this shape.

Unchanged outline (135,191 km2) as Mayapan becomes the capital: 'from the 1220s until the 1440s', leading 'a group of allies that included much of the northern Yucatan'. Mayapan itself is 4.2 km2 and 10,000-17,000 people, so the shape is the area of the Mayapan allies and the Yucatecan provinces, not a territory the city held.
A single-cell flicker (about 56 km2 of area) in 1429-1430 near Lamanai (17.7 N); no page speaks to it and it is not an event.
Back to the 135,191 km2 outline for 1431-1439; the flicker of 1429 is gone. Mayapan stands until the Xiu revolt: 'In 1441, Ah Xiu Xupan of the powerful noble family of Xiu became resentful'.

Again the one-cell variant (135,135 km2) for 1440-1449, while Mayapan falls: the Cocom 'were killed', the city 'sacked and abandoned' (written records 1441, archaeology tentatively 1461) and 'Yucatan devolved into warring city-states'. Cliopatria does not split the shape; the successors are the Yucatecan provinces, which have no dossiers yet.

187,745 km2: the shape grows by about 201 cells southward (central Peten around Tikal and Tayasal, the Belize-Peten lowlands, Cozumel and Zaculeu). The Mayapan page does not date or name this; the Itza, expelled from Mayapan, are at Lake Peten Itza from about 1441-1446 (itza-mayans dossier, Nojpeten page), and Zaculeu is the highland Mam capital that fell in 1525 (Maya civilization). Kept as Cliopatria draws it; the Itza core should be drawn over it from 1441.

182,719 km2: Zaculeu and Cozumel drop out (about 20 cells). The page has 'the fall of Zaculeu, the Mam Maya capital, in 1525', a year earlier than the shape; Cozumel is not reached by Montejo until the second half of September 1527 (Spanish conquest of Yucatan), so its removal in 1526 is page-silent.

170,075 km2: about 49 cells of the southwest (bbox 91.6-90.3 W, 15.3-18.3 N, no named centre inside) drop out in 1529. The conquest page has Montejo pacify Tabasco in 1529 and Alonso d'Avila sent to Acalan, with 'Salamanca de Acalan' founded in 1530, which may be this area; the page does not say.

170,356 km2: a one-cell change in 1534. Not an event. The page's 1534 is the year Montejo the Younger 'was forced to abandon Chichen Itza' and the Spanish left Campeche (end 1534 or start 1535), so the shape correctly stays whole.

Unchanged outline to 1546, although the page has the first permanent Spanish town councils at Campeche and Merida in 1541-42 and the 'final conquest of the northern portion' only in late 1546; the ledger records the 1541 and 1546 steps. The Peten part of the shape is the Itza kingdom, which stayed independent to 1697.

region.text: the northern lowlands and the central Peten

ledger.note: 850: the Maya city-states continue in the north and the central lowlands after the southern kingdoms fall. 'The Northern Yucatan in particular prospered afterwards'; 'population centers continued in many coastal regions and in the northern Yucatan Peninsula, including Chichen Itza, Uxmal, and Coba'. The year 850 is Cliopatria's second Maya row; no page dates a break.

region.text: the central Peten and the Palenque country abandoned after the Terminal Classic

ledger.note: 960: the central lowlands (Tikal, El Mirador, Uaxactun, Palenque) drop out. 'Palenque, Copan, Tikal, and Calakmul went into decline during the 8th and 9th centuries and were abandoned shortly thereafter'; the Tikal page: 'After 950, Tikal was all but deserted'. The year 960 is Cliopatria's.

1221: the seat of the northern Maya passes from Chichen Itza to Mayapan. Mayapan was the capital 'from the 1220s until the 1440s' and 'some sources say that the Maya revolted in 1221 against the Maya-Toltec lords of Chichen Itza'; the Chichen Itza page says that city 'declined as a regional center by 1100, before the rise of Mayapan' and gives only 'the 13th century' for Hunac Ceel. The destination is Mayapan (20.63 N 89.46 W).

region.text: the central Peten around Lake Peten Itza, the Belize-Peten lowlands, Cozumel and the Zaculeu country added in 1450

ledger.note: 1450: the shape grows southward by about 201 cells to take in the central Peten (Tayasal), Zaculeu's country and Cozumel. The Mayapan page is silent on it; the Itza, expelled from Mayapan, build Nojpeten on Lake Peten Itza in the mid-15th century (itza-mayans dossier). The year 1450 is Cliopatria's.

region.text: Zaculeu and the Cozumel cells that leave the shape in 1526

ledger.note: 1525: Zaculeu, the Mam capital, falls to the Spanish. 'This was followed by the fall of Zaculeu, the Mam Maya capital, in 1525'. The land is in Cliopatria's shape from 1450 and leaves it in 1526; the Mam are a highland people, not a lowland city-state.

region.text: the Ekab coast near Xelha, where the Spanish first held ground

ledger.note: 1527: the first campaign of Francisco de Montejo lands on the east coast. 'He left Spain with 400 men in four ships' and 'made landfall somewhere near Xelha' in Ekab after reaching Cozumel in the second half of September; Xelha was garrisoned (Salamanca de Xelha) before the garrison was destroyed in 1528.

region.text: the southwestern fringe (Acalan and the Usumacinta country) that Cliopatria drops in 1529

ledger.note: 1529: about 49 cells of the southwest leave the shape. The conquest page has Montejo 'pacified that province [Tabasco] with the aid of his son' and Avila sent to conquer Acalan in 1529, with Salamanca de Acalan founded in 1530; it does not tie either to these cells.

region.text: the east coast near Xelha, the Campeche coast and Chichen Itza, where Montejo's bases stood in 1527-1534

ledger.note: 1535: the Spanish are out of the peninsula but for Champotón. 'The Spanish retreated from Campeche to Veracruz' at the end of 1534 or the start of 1535 after Montejo the Younger 'was forced to abandon Chichen Itza in 1534'; 'Champotón was by now the last Spanish outpost in Yucatan'.

region.text: Campeche and Merida (T'ho), with Mani (the Xiu) as the Spanish ally

ledger.note: 1541: the Spanish return to stay. 'The first permanent Spanish town councils in the entire peninsula were founded at Campeche and Merida' in 1541-42 (T'ho became Merida); the Xiu Maya of Mani allied with the Spanish, and 'his submission to Spain and conversion to Christianity encouraged the lords of the western provinces'. The page gives no date for the Xiu alliance.

region.text: the northern Yucatan Peninsula and the Campeche and Quintana Roo coasts

ledger.note: 1546: the last Maya resistance in the north is broken. 'In late 1546 an alliance of eastern provinces launched an unsuccessful uprising against the Spanish'; it was defeated in a single battle, which 'marked the final conquest of the northern portion' of the peninsula.

region.text: the northern Yucatan Peninsula and the Campeche and Quintana Roo coasts, without the Itza lands of the Peten

ledger.note: 1546: the northern Yucatan passes to the Spanish. Final conquest of the northern portion in 1546 (Spanish conquest of Yucatan; Maya civilization: 'finally completed the conquest of the northern portion of the peninsula in 1546'). The Peten core of Cliopatria's shape (the Itza kingdom) stays independent.
1546: the last of the northern Maya provinces is conquered and the Postclassic Maya city-states end; only the Itza of the Peten remain free, to 1697.

wars.name: Spanish conquest of Yucatán

zones.text: the northern Yucatan Peninsula and the Campeche and Quintana Roo coasts

wars.outcome: Spanish victory after three attempts (1527-1528, 1531-1535, 1540-1546): permanent towns at Campeche and Merida in 1541-42, the Xiu of Mani allied with Spain, and the eastern provinces defeated in late 1546.
wars.note: The Xiu-Cocom feud and the Cupul-Chikinchel salt-bed feud divided the provinces. The conquest page does not date the Xiu alliance.

wars.name: Overthrow of Mayapan
wars.outcome: The Xiu revolted against the Cocom rulers of Mayapan; the Cocom were massacred and the city abandoned (1441 by written records, about 1461 by archaeology); the northern Yucatan broke into warring provinces. No border of the Cliopatria shape moved.
wars.note: Internal to the shape. Mayapan page: 'all of the Cocom family, except one who was away in Honduras conducting trade, were killed'.

certainty.note: No surveyed or treaty frontier: the shape is the envelope of the Puuc and Chichen Itza states, the Mayapan allies and the Yucatecan provinces; the Spanish towns of 1541-42 are points, not borders.

notes:
TWO ROWS, ONE ARTICLE. This row (850..1546) and 'Mayan City-States' (-247..849) share Wikidata Q28567; they are kept as two dossiers (see the notes of mayan-city-states). The shape is an envelope: Chichen Itza, Uxmal and the Puuc states, the Mayapan confederacy (a 'group of allies that included much of the northern Yucatan'), the sixteen to twenty-four Yucatecan provinces of the Spanish conquest page ('Yucatan devolved into warring city-states') and, from 1450, the Itza of Lake Peten Itza all sit inside it. Dossiers written in this batch for the individual states: chichen-itza, mayapan and itza-mayans (kept from an earlier run). The provinces (Mani/Xiu, Sotuta/Cocom, Cupul, Chetumal, Ah Canul, Campeche, Champoton, Ecab, Cochuah, Chikinchel, Tases, Hocaba, Ceh Pech, Ah Kin Chel, Uaymil, Acalan) have no dossiers; see counterparts_needing_dossiers in the report.
CAPITAL. The shape has no capital in any page; Chichen Itza and Mayapan are used as label anchors for the eras the pages call them regional capitals; 1449-1546 has no seat. Cliopatria's Seshat ids for this row are gt_tikal_terminal_classic and gt_tikal_early_postclassic.
THE 960 AND 1450 STEPS. Both are Cliopatria's years and no page dates them (confidence 1). The 1450 growth is the Itza core of the Peten, Cozumel and Zaculeu; the Itza dossier starts the Itza in 1441, so renderers should draw itza-mayans over this shape from 1441.
SPANISH CONQUEST. Cliopatria keeps the whole shape to 1546 although the Spanish held Xelha, Campeche, Chichen Itza and Champoton in 1527-1535 and Campeche and Merida from 1541-42; the ledger models that as two contest spans (1527-1535, 1541-1546) with the loss in 1546. The Xiu of Mani 'allied themselves with the Spanish' (page gives no year), so Mani was a Spanish ally before 1546; a gap-filler could open 'Tutul Xiu' or 'Mani' to date it. The 1546 uprising of the eastern provinces is not called the 'Great Maya Revolt' on the page.
PAGE BUDGET (5): Maya civilization, Classic Maya collapse, Chichen Itza, Mayapan, Spanish conquest of Yucatan. Not opened: Mayapan's league sources, Postclassic Yucatan provinces page, Tulum, Cozumel, Itza pages (the earlier run's Nojpeten and Itza pages are cited only through the itza-mayans dossier). The Tikal and Calakmul pages opened for mayan-city-states were used for two notes (869, 909, 950).
INFOBOX AREA. None of the five pages gives an area for the Postclassic Maya; Mayapan city is 4.2 km2 against the shape's 135,000-188,000 km2, again showing the shape is an envelope.
GAZETTEER. All names resolve (Tulum, Campeche, Mérida, Chichen Itza, the three admin-1 units).
